description: Tween Eye:building one consistent wildfire record from two satellites. We’re tackling “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” by merging NASA FIRMS data into a burning-activity calendar with anomaly detection for early warning. I bring a strong background in software, data and AI/ML. Looking for: Earth science or remote sensing knowledge, a front-end/web developer, a designer for a clean interface, and someone to craft the pitch and demo. All skill levels welcome. Join us!
summary: Tween Eye is a web application and data pipeline that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning activity calendar. MODIS gives more than two decades of history but is being retired, while VIIRS offers finer detail from 2012; their different resolution, sensitivity and schedules make the records impossible to compare directly. We match the sensors by overpass time, aggregate detections to a common grid, calibrate VIIRS to MODIS over fourteen overlapping years, and stitch them into a single series from 2002 to 2026. The harmonized record shows no jump at the switch, and tested on years it never saw, the error is about 17%. Using British Columbia as a demonstration, emergency managers can draw an area, choose dates, view a color-blind-safe calendar of monthly activity, see anomalies against the historical median, compare any year with the seasonal norm, and download the data as CSV. This matters because fire managers need a trustworthy baseline to recognize unusual conditions early; harmonization keeps two decades of history usable as MODIS ends.
details:
What it does and how it works: Tween Eye is a data pipeline plus a web application. The pipeline takes NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from Aqua MODIS (2002 onward) and Suomi-NPP VIIRS (2012 onward) and builds one sensor-independent record. It keeps detections of comparable quality, counts them per 0.25° grid cell per month, learns a scale factor between the sensors over fourteen years of overlap, and stitches MODIS before 2012 to scaled VIIRS after. The web app reads the result. Users draw an area on the map or type coordinates, choose a date range, and see a year-by-month calendar of burning activity as counts or as anomalies against the historical median, with a bold line marking the sensor switch. A seasonal chart compares any year with the norm, and the data downloads as CSV or PNG.

Benefits: Emergency managers keep a trustworthy two-decade baseline as MODIS is retired. They can see which months and years burned most, and whether the current month is unusual for their area.

Evidence: The two sensors correlate at 0.988 monthly. Leaving each year out and predicting it gives a 17% error. There is no step in the series at the 2012 switch, and it recovers British Columbia’s record years (2017, 2018, 2021 and 2023).

Intended impact: Earlier recognition of abnormal fire conditions, better planning of monitoring effort, and a method that can be repeated for other regions, since it only needs a FIRMS download and an optional boundary file.

Tools: Python (pandas, NumPy) for the pipeline, and HTML, JavaScript, Leaflet, Leaflet.draw and Papa Parse for the app. Data and boundaries came from NASA FIRMS and Natural Earth, the base map is OpenStreetMap, and the code is on GitHub with the site hosted on Netlify. No special hardware was needed.

Creativity: We tested the harmonization instead of just asserting it. Fire radiative power agrees between sensors (factor about 1.13) even though hotspot counts differ tenfold, which confirms the sensors see the same fires. A fixed-source filter removes gas flares, an anomaly guard hides misleading percentages in quiet months, and a square-root, color-blind-safe scale keeps extreme years from washing out the rest.

Factors we considered: Honesty about limits (hotspots are not burned area, recent months are provisional, and autumn burning is mostly human-caused), simplicity of explanation (one scale factor beat month-by-month factors out of sample), and accessibility for responders who need to read the calendar quickly.
